The Enugu State House of Assembly on Tuesday passed the Landlord and Tenant Amendment Bill, introducing strict statutory limits on rent increments and overhauling tenancy regulations across the state. The legislation, formally titled “A Bill for a Law to Amend the Landlord and Tenant Second Amendment Bill, Cap. 101, Revised Laws of Enugu State 2024 (House Bill No. 3, 2025),” scaled third reading following the adoption of a joint review report presented during plenary. Under the newly passed provisions, landlords are barred from increasing rent until after a minimum period of four years, with any subsequent upward review strictly capped at two per cent of the prevailing rent. However, where a property owner executes verifiable, substantial renovations, the bill permits an upward review of not more than 10 per cent. The bill’s passage followed a motion moved by the member representing Nkanu West Constituency, Hon. Iloabuchi Abugu, and seconded by the Deputy Speaker and member representing Awgu North Constituency, Rt. Hon. Jane Eneh, after which the House dissolved into the Committee of the Whole for clause-by-clause consideration. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Okey Mbah (Nkanu East), stated that the legislation was the product of extensive stakeholder consultations. Mbah described the bill as a game-changer designed to curb arbitrary charges and protect residents from exploitation by property owners and middlemen. “This bill will subsidise over 60 per cent of what residents used to pay while trying to secure accommodation,” the lawmaker stated. Hon. Uche Ugwu, hailed the legislation as a milestone in the state’s good governance agenda, noting that it would grant tenants across Enugu State a new lease of life. “This law is going to address all the cries of residents about the escalating rent in the state,” he said. The bill, which passed its second reading on March 11, 2026, and underwent a public hearing on March 26, 2026, now awaits the assent of Governor Peter Mbah to become law. The legislative intervention comes amid widespread public outcry across Enugu metropolis and surrounding urban centres over soaring house rents, arbitrary agent commissions, and exorbitant legal fees that have priced low- and middle-income earners out of decent housing. While tenant groups have welcomed the move, the legislation has already triggered pushback from property owners, who argue that fixed rent caps ignore prevailing macroeconomic realities, high building material costs, and inflationary pressures. Reacting to the development, a landlord in the state capital, Johnson Onyekwere, dismissed the two per cent cap as unrealistic and unenforceable given the current economic climate. Onyekwere said, “That would have been a natural law if the prices of petroleum products and electricity tariffs increased by two per cent. Otherwise, it is an unnatural law. It is neither sustainable nor can it be obeyed. “You cannot single out landlords and regulate their business while other sectors are struggling to meet the benchmark of inflation set by the managers of the Nigerian economy. It violates landlords’ rights against discrimination,” he stated. Raphael Ede
